# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

An incident leaves traces in four places. Metrics tell you **when** and **how much**, logs tell you **what**, traces tell you **where**, and change events tell you **why now**. Engineers who look at only one of them guess; engineers who link them by time and by trace ID find the cause in minutes.

In this lab you receive the telemetry of one real-looking incident as files: per-minute metrics for four services, error and info log lines with trace IDs, a set of sampled traces and a change-event log. You detect the anomaly, count the failing log lines, follow one failed request through its trace, decide which of two changes is the trigger, and write the root cause statement.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can take a symptom from a user complaint to a named trigger without asking another team. |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You move from metric to log to trace using time and trace\_id instead of guessing. |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: You write a root cause statement that says what changed, where, and what users saw. |

## 1.2  Lab Scenario

| 📢  Incident Briefing — Checkout Is Slow and Failing |
| :---- |
| TIME: 10:12 UTC │ PRIORITY: HIGH │ ASSIGNED TO: You |
| REQUEST RECEIVED: "Customers report that checkout hangs for several seconds and then shows an error. It started a few minutes ago. Two things changed this morning. Tell us which one caused it and why." |
| CONTEXT: The shop has four services: frontend, checkout, payment and inventory. The incident bundle holds metrics (metrics.csv), logs (logs.jsonl), 24 sampled traces (traces.json) and the change events (events.log). All times are UTC on 2026-11-23. |
| YOUR MISSION: Find the first bad minute, quantify the damage, trace one failed checkout, name the trigger and write the root cause statement. You have 28 minutes for the core tasks. |

*Figure: Day 6 Lab 1 — Starting Environment: Terminal in the lab1-correlation Folder; Four Data Files (metrics.csv, logs.jsonl, traces.json, events.log) and the Helper q.py*

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

The same incident looks different in each signal. The links between them are the **time** (metrics ↔ logs ↔ events) and the **trace\_id** (logs ↔ traces).

*Figure: Correlation Map — Metric Anomaly (when, how much) → Log Lines (what) → Trace (where) → Change Event (why now) → Root Cause Statement*

| Signal | What It Holds | How You Query It Here | Typical Question |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Metrics | Per-minute requests, error %, p95 latency, DB pool usage per service | python3 q.py metrics | When did it start and how bad is it? |
| Logs | One JSON line per event with level, service, message and trace\_id | python3 q.py logs | What error message do users get? |
| Traces | Spans per request with service, operation, duration and status | python3 q.py trace \<id\> | Which downstream call was slow or failed? |
| Change events | Deployments and configuration changes with time and service | python3 q.py events | What changed just before the problem? |

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

• Detect the start and size of a metric anomaly from per-minute data

• Count and group error log lines by service and message

• Follow a trace ID from a log line to its spans and find the slow or failing span

• Place change events on the incident timeline and rule out an unrelated change

• Distinguish symptom, trigger and root cause

• Write a root cause statement with what changed, where and the user effect

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| DO NOT edit the data files — they are your evidence. |
| DO NOT guess a cause from the most recent visible change; prove it with time and service. |
| DO NOT use real credentials or touch any live system; this lab needs none. |
| DO NOT share your answers before the debrief. |

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Symptom, Trigger and Root Cause

**Symptom** is what users or dashboards show (checkout slow, 504 errors). **Trigger** is the event that started the problem (a change, a deployment, a traffic jump). **Root cause** is the mechanism that connects the trigger to the symptom (why the change hurt users). A good statement names all three.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| The trigger is what you roll back; the root cause is what you fix permanently; the symptom is what you tell customers. Mixing them up leads to the wrong action. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Correlation by Time vs Proof by Mechanism

Two events near the problem are both suspects. The one that touches the failing service and happened **before** the first bad minute is the candidate; the other must be ruled out with evidence (different service, no change in its own metrics, wrong time).

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake During Investigations |
| :---- |
| Blaming the most recent deployment because it is the most visible. Always check the time (before the first bad minute?) and the service (does it touch the failing path?). |

## 3.3  Helper Commands You Need

| Command | What It Shows | Useful Options |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| python3 q.py metrics | Per-minute metrics | \--service checkout \--from 10:00 \--to 10:20 |
| python3 q.py logs | Log lines (first 20\) | \--service S \--level ERROR \--count \--limit 5 \--contains TEXT |
| python3 q.py traces / trace \<id\> | Sampled trace ids / spans of one trace | — |
| python3 q.py events | Change events | — |

# 4\. LAB TASKS

*Figure: Day 6 Lab 1 — Four-Task Investigation Workflow: Metrics → Logs → Trace → Events and Root Cause*

| TASK 1 — METRICS: Find the Start and Size of the Anomaly |
| :---- |

| 1 | Detect the anomaly in per-minute metrics | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

You compare the healthy baseline with the incident minutes for checkout, then look at the frontend and payment to see who is affected.

| ⌨  Task 1 — Read the metrics |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: checkout during the incident |
| python3 q.py metrics \--service checkout \--from 10:05 \--to 10:15 ![][image7] |
| \# Step 2: the neighbours |
| python3 q.py metrics \--service payment \--from 10:05 \--to 10:15 ![][image8] |
| python3 q.py metrics \--service frontend \--from 10:05 \--to 10:15 ![][image9] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: 10:05-10:07 error\_pct 0.0-0.4, p95 ≈ 380-480 ms · 10:08-10:12 error\_pct \= 25.0, p95 ≈ 4678 ms · 10:13 back to normal |
| Step 2: payment error\_pct ≈ 30 and p95 ≈ 3000 ms in 10:08-10:12 |
| Step 3: frontend error\_pct ≈ 4.0 (small) and p95 about normal |
| **1.A Record the first bad minute, the last bad minute, the peak checkout p95 and the peak error %.**  Answer: First bad minute 10:08, last bad minute 10:12 (five minutes). Peak checkout p95 4778 ms (normal ≈ 430 ms) and peak error rate 25.0 %. |
| **1.B The frontend error rate is only about 4 % while checkout shows 25 %. Why is the number smaller at the frontend?**  Answer: The frontend serves many routes (products, cart, checkout); only the checkout share of its traffic fails, so its overall error rate is diluted. The checkout route itself is the symptom. |

| TASK 2 — LOGS: Count and Group the Errors |
| :---- |

| 2 | Read the error log lines | ⏱ 8 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Logs show what the failing service says. You count the ERROR lines per service, read the messages and copy one trace ID.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Query the logs |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: how many ERROR lines per service |
| python3 q.py logs \--service checkout \--level ERROR \--count ![][image10] |
| python3 q.py logs \--service payment \--level ERROR \--count ![][image11] |
| python3 q.py logs \--service frontend \--level ERROR \--count ![][image12] |
| \# Step 2: the messages |
| python3 q.py logs \--service checkout \--level ERROR \--limit 3 ![][image13] |
| python3 q.py logs \--service payment \--level ERROR \--limit 3 ![][image14] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: checkout 117 · payment 140 · frontend 128 |
| Step 2 checkout: "Checkout failed: payment gateway timeout (504)" |
| Step 2 payment: "PSP call exceeded timeout after 3000ms" — every line carries a 32-character trace\_id |
| **2.A Record the three ERROR counts and the two messages. Which service reports the root of the problem and which only reports the consequence?**  Answer: checkout 117, payment 140, frontend 128\. Payment reports the root (the call to the payment provider exceeded 3000 ms); checkout and frontend only report the consequence (gateway timeout 504, upstream 504). |
| **2.B Why does the payment service have more ERROR lines than checkout?**  Answer: Payment logs one line for each failed call to the provider, including calls repeated for the same order, while checkout logs one line per failed checkout. More failed calls than failed checkouts is expected. |

| TASK 3 — TRACES: Follow One Failed Checkout |
| :---- |

| 3 | Open a failed trace and find the slow span | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Only some traces are stored (sampled). You list the stored trace IDs and open one where the payment span takes 3000 ms.

| ⌨  Task 3 — Read a trace |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: stored trace ids |
| python3 q.py traces ![][image15] |
| \# Step 2: open a failed checkout trace (this one has the 3000 ms payment span) |
| python3 q.py trace 64bcb999c7ae20a66b538666c747eb5d ![][image16] |
| \# Step 3: compare with a normal trace (the last ids in the list are healthy)  ![][image17] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: 24 trace ids (12 failed, 12 healthy) |
| Step 2: frontend POST /api/checkout 4720 ms ERROR · checkout checkout.create 4700 ms ERROR · inventory stock.reserve 80 ms OK · payment psp.charge 3000 ms ERROR |
| Step 3: healthy trace: frontend 410 ms · checkout 380 ms · payment psp.charge 240 ms OK |
| **3.A Which span is the slow or failing one, and how do you know the other spans are not the cause?**  Answer: payment psp.charge: 3000 ms with status ERROR. The inventory span is 80 ms OK, and the checkout and frontend spans are long only because they wait for the payment span. |
| **3.B Why can you open this trace from a log line?**  Answer: Every log line has a trace\_id, the same ID that identifies the trace; searching the trace store with that ID returns all spans of the request. |

| TASK 4 — EVENTS AND ROOT CAUSE: Trigger, Unrelated Change, Statement |
| :---- |

| 4 | Find the trigger and write the root cause statement | ⏱ 6 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Two events are in the log. You decide which one started the problem and which one is a coincidence, then write the statement.

| ⌨  Task 4 — Change events |
| :---- |
|  |
| python3 q.py events ![][image18] |
| \# Compare each event time with the first bad minute (10:08) and its service with the failing service (payment) |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| 09:40 DEP-4410 frontend deployment  frontend 4.1.2 rolled out (CSS and banner change) |
| 10:06 CHG-2201 payment config-change  payment client timeout 1000 ms \-\> 3000 ms |
| **4.A Which event is the trigger and which is unrelated? Give the evidence for each.**  Answer: Trigger: `CHG-2201` (payment client timeout `1000 → 3000 ms`) at `10:06`, two minutes before the first bad minute (`10:08`) and in the failing `payment` service. Unrelated: `DEP-4410` (`frontend 4.1.2`) at `09:40`, 28 minutes earlier, affecting only CSS/banner on `frontend`, whose metrics remained normal afterward.  |
| **4.B Write the root cause statement (what changed, where, what users saw).**  Answer: At `10:06`, `CHG-2201` raised the `payment` client timeout from `1000 ms` to `3000 ms`; from `10:08` to `10:12`, payment provider calls stalled until the `3000 ms` timeout and failed, causing `checkout` to wait \~3 s per attempt and return `504` errors for \~`25%` of checkouts.  |
| **4.C What is the symptom, the trigger and the root cause in your statement?**  Answer: Symptom: slow checkout (\~`4778 ms` peak p95) and `504` errors (\~`25%`). Trigger: `CHG-2201` timeout configuration change at `10:06`. Root cause: slow payment provider calls now wait the full `3000 ms` before failing, holding upstream `checkout` requests until they time out.  |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| python3: command not found | Python missing or named python on Windows | python3 \--version / python \--version | Use python; install Python 3.8+ |
| No such file data/metrics.csv | Terminal in the wrong folder | ls | cd into lab1-correlation |
| trace not found | Only sampled traces are stored | python3 q.py traces | Pick an id from the list |
| Counts differ from the guide | Edited data files or wrong service filter | re-copy the folder | Use \--service checkout \--level ERROR \--count |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Metrics, Logs and Traces Together |
| :---- |
| Why did the metric alone not tell you the cause? |
| Which link (time or trace\_id) did you use to move from logs to the trace? |
| Key insight: Each signal answers one question; the links turn them into one story. |

| Discussion 2 — The Unrelated Change |
| :---- |
| Why is the frontend deployment tempting? |
| What two checks ruled it out? |
| Key insight: Check time and service before blaming a change. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Blaming the latest deployment | It is the most visible change | Wrong rollback, problem stays | Check time and service |
| Reading only the metric | Fast to look at | Symptom without cause | Pivot to logs and traces |
| Using the first trace in the list | Healthy traces look normal | No failing span found | Pick a trace from a failing log line |
| Writing 'timeout' only | Short statement feels enough | No action possible | Say what changed and where |
